sections.title: The Committee's Work
sections.content:
At the Network Working Group meeting in Urbana on February 17 to 19, 1971, a committee was formed to review the Host/Host protocol. Steve Crocker chaired the committee, which had eight other members.

The group reached consensus on some proposed changes, while other topics remained unresolved. It planned to ask the network community for reactions and reconvene at UCLA on March 8 before deciding on final recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: A committee reviewed the Host/Host protocol and agreed on some proposed changes. It planned to ask network participants for comments before making final recommendations.

sections.title: Agreed Recommendations
sections.content:
The committee recommends changing the lengths of several commands, removing Message Data Types and the Cease mechanism, and adding one-byte reset and reset-reply commands. RST would clear NCP table entries associated with the sending host; RRP would acknowledge the reset. The committee recommends against changing connections to full-duplex.

It also recommends messages made of whole bytes, with a 16-bit byte count and an 8-bit byte-size field. The report discusses handling console interrupts through an INS signal and a network-wide special code.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee proposes several command changes, including a reset request and reply. It also recommends that messages state how many bytes they contain and the size of each byte.

sections.title: Questions Still Open
sections.content:
The committee did not settle whether control messages should have a special length limit. It lists two possible limits: no special limit, about 1000 bytes, or a limit of 120 bytes. It also leaves open where the first data byte should begin, comparing a single transmission with a two-transmission approach.

For flow control, the report presents leaving the existing allocation commands unchanged or tracking both message counts and bit counts. In the latter option, the sender could not let either counter go below zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The report leaves several design choices open, including control-message length, message layout and whether flow control should count messages and bits separately.
